passages.heading: Speech fallback chain
passages.text:
piper (CLI or the piper-tts package, and a voice in the voices folder) → espeak-ng →
espeak → say (macOS) → sapi (Windows) → silent. In the silent case JEV writes a silent
track of the estimated speaking time (about 155 words per minute). Captions then carry the narration,
and the tool result says so in plain words. Text reaches every engine through a file or stdin, never
on the command line.

passages.heading: Piper voices: where to get them, and checksums
passages.text:
Voices are published at https://huggingface.co/rhasspy/piper-voices (you can listen to samples at
https://rhasspy.github.io/piper-samples/). Each voice is two files, <name>.onnx and
<name>.onnx.json, e.g. en_US-lessac-medium.

* With JEV (asks first): download_voice fetches both files from the pinned revision v1.0.0
  over HTTPS (only huggingface.co and its CDN subdomains are allowed). It checks each file's size
  and MD5 against voices.json from the same revision and only saves files that match. It then
  records each file's SHA-256 in voices-manifest.json, which is checked every time the voice is
  used, so a corrupted or swapped file is refused.
* By hand: put both files in the voices folder (~/.jev/voices; change it with
  media.voices_dir or JEV_VOICES_DIR). To pin them, add
  {"<name>.onnx": {"sha256": "<sha256sum output>"}} to voices-manifest.json.
* Recommended: en_US-lessac-medium (clear, neutral), en_US-amy-medium, en_US-ryan-high,
  en_GB-alan-medium.

Licence note: piper-tts 1.3 and later (the OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl project) is GPL-3.0. JEV only
calls it as an optional external program or package. Each voice has its own licence on its model
card.

passages.text:
VRAM figures are approximate peaks at fp16/bf16 and depend on resolution, frame count and diffusers
version. JEV picks "fully on GPU" when the card has the first figure and model CPU offload when it
has the second. Otherwise it refuses and names the model and both figures: "needs ~N GB of GPU
memory (~M GB with CPU offload); this GPU has X GB".

Rules:

passages.heading: Generative models
passages.text:
* Weights only from folders you chose: <models_dir>/<name> (media.models_dir,
  JEV_MODELS_DIR, default ~/.jev/models), or a name mapped to any folder with
  media.model_dirs. The model can only pass a catalog or folder name, never a path.
* Safetensors only. A pickle checkpoint (.bin/.ckpt/.pt/.pth/.pkl/..., the same list as
  jepa_studio.weights) is refused, and so is a component that has only pickle weights. Stray
  pickles next to safetensors are reported and never read (use_safetensors=True). A
  model_index.json whose pipeline class is not on the allowlist (SDXL/SD/SD3, FLUX, LTX, Wan) is
  refused, so custom pipeline code is never run.
* Offline loading: HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 and local_files_only=True.
* Downloads (approval): download_generative_model uses huggingface_hub.snapshot_download
  with allow-patterns for JSON, text, tokenizer files and *.safetensors (the fp16 variant for
  SDXL-Turbo), and ignore-patterns for every pickle and other format. It deletes any pickle that
  arrives anyway, then records each file's SHA-256 in jev-model.json. Those hashes are verified
  before each load.
* No text-to-video on CPU. A few seconds of video means dozens of denoising steps through a
  multi-billion-parameter transformer over every frame. On a CPU that takes many hours, so JEV
  refuses with that explanation. Image generation on CPU is allowed only for sdxl-turbo.
* Deterministic: a torch.Generator seeded with seed. The same seed, model, versions and
  hardware give the same output. Every output gets a .json sidecar (and PNG text metadata) with
  the prompt, seed, steps, model, device and licence.

passages.heading: How FFmpeg is run
passages.text:
FFmpeg is found on PATH, else the imageio-ffmpeg binary is used. It always runs from an argument
list, never a shell, with -nostdin. Every file input must resolve inside the workspace and is
passed as file:<absolute path> with -protocol_whitelist file. Inputs that look like URLs or
protocols (http://, concat:, subfile:) are refused. Filter graphs that open files or load
plugins (movie=, amovie=, textfile=, file=, ladspa, sendcmd, lut3d, ...) are refused,
and a subtitles= file must be inside the workspace. Progress comes from -progress pipe:1, and
cancelling or timing out terminates the process and removes the partial output.

passages.heading: Honest limits
passages.text:
* espeak-ng sounds robotic. It is clear but not natural. Install Piper and a voice for natural
  narration.
* Shot detection finds hard cuts reliably. Slow dissolves and fades may be missed or placed late.
  Search takes an image or a moment of the video, not a text query, because no local text-image
  model ships here.
* With stream copy (lossless, fast), the start of each cut is keyframe-exact and the end is cut by
  frame count. With sources that use B-frames, the last frame or two can differ from a re-encode.
  mode=reencode is frame-accurate. auto copies only when every cut starts on a keyframe and
  nothing is drawn on top.
* A clip's own audio is not used inside explainers (the narration track is). Cut lists keep the
  source audio.
* The render estimate is a rough CPU figure. Generative model timings vary a lot between GPUs.
* The generative adapters are tested here with an injected fake pipeline, because no weights can be
  downloaded on the CI machine. The real diffusers path follows the documented APIs, but it has not
  been run end to end on a GPU in this repo's tests.

* Cut list (*.cuts.json, jev-cutlist/v1): source, fps, cuts `{start, end, label, reason,
  score, record_start, record_end}. The EDL (*.edl`) holds the same cuts in CMX3600 form,

passages.heading: 1. The physics
passages.text:
Units are geometrized, $G = c = 1$, and the black-hole mass is $M = 1$, so lengths and times are in
units of $M$ ($1\,M = GM/c^2 \approx 1.5$ km per solar mass).

passages.heading: Spacetime and light rays
passages.text:
The Kerr metric in Boyer–Lindquist coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with spin $a = J/M$, uses

$$\Sigma = r^2 + a^2\cos^2\theta,\qquad \Delta = r^2 - 2Mr + a^2,\qquad A = (r^2+a^2)^2 - a^2\Delta\sin^2\theta .$$

A photon has three conserved quantities (Carter 1968): energy $E$, axial angular momentum $L$ and
the Carter constant $Q$. With $b = L/E$, $q = Q/E^2$ and the Mino time $d\sigma = d\lambda/\Sigma$ the
geodesic equations separate:

$$\left(\frac{dr}{d\sigma}\right)^2 = R(r) = \left(r^2 + a^2 - ab\right)^2 - \Delta\left[(b-a)^2 + q\right]$$

$$\left(\frac{d\theta}{d\sigma}\right)^2 = \Theta(\theta) = q + a^2\cos^2\theta - b^2\cot^2\theta$$

$$\frac{d\phi}{d\sigma} = \frac{a\,(r^2 + a^2 - ab)}{\Delta} + \frac{b}{\sin^2\theta} - a,\qquad
\frac{dt}{d\sigma} = \frac{(r^2+a^2)(r^2+a^2-ab)}{\Delta} + a\,(b - a\sin^2\theta).$$

How they are integrated. The square roots in the first-order form need sign bookkeeping at every
radial and polar turning point. The renderer instead integrates the second-order form

$$\frac{d^2r}{d\sigma^2} = \tfrac12 R'(r),\qquad \frac{d^2\theta}{d\sigma^2} = \tfrac12\Theta'(\theta),$$

passages.heading: Spacetime and light rays
passages.text:
which passes smoothly through turning points, with an adaptive Dormand–Prince 5(4) method. Each ray has
its own step size, and all rays advance together as torch tensors, so a frame is one batched
computation (on the GPU when there is one). Finished rays are dropped from the batch as they go.
After each accepted step the velocities are projected back onto the exact first integrals,
$v_r \leftarrow \operatorname{sign}(v_r)\sqrt{R}$ and $v_\theta \leftarrow \operatorname{sign}(v_\theta)\sqrt{\Theta}$, except
near turning points. This matters for far cameras: at $r = 1000\,M$ the information about $b$ sits in a
relative difference of $10^{-6}$ between $v_r^2$ and $r^4$. Without the projection the shadow edge of an
$a = 0.99$ hole came out wrong by 2.5 M; with it, it agrees to $10^{-4}$ (section 3).

passages.heading: Spacetime and light rays
passages.text:
Termination per ray: captured when it is moving inward inside $r_+ + \tfrac12(r_{\rm ph}^{\rm pro} - r_+)$
(no radial turning point is left there); escaped when it is moving outward beyond
$\max(1.5\,r_{\rm cam}, 2\,r_{\rm out}, 100\,M)$. In that case the direction at infinity is the ray continued
as a straight line in the flat oblate-spheroidal coordinates that Boyer–Lindquist become for
$M \to 0$, plus the first-order remaining bending $\tfrac34 M l^3/r^4$ ($l^2 = q + b^2$). The residual is
below $10^{-6}$ rad. Rays that hit neither within the step budget are reported as unresolved in the
JSON (0 in every render below).

passages.heading: The camera
passages.text:
As in James et al. (2015), the camera is at rest in the locally non-rotating frame of the
zero-angular-momentum observer (ZAMO, which they call the FIDO). Its lapse, frame-dragging angular
velocity and circumferential radius are

$$\alpha = \sqrt{\Sigma\Delta/A},\qquad \omega = 2aMr/A,\qquad \varpi = \sqrt{A/\Sigma}\,\sin\theta .$$

A pixel's direction $\mathbf n$ in the camera frame (forward $=-\mathbf e_r$, right $=\mathbf e_\phi$,
up $=-\mathbf e_\theta$, so the spin axis points up in the image) gives the photon's momenta for ZAMO
energy 1:

$$p_r = -n_r\sqrt{\Sigma/\Delta},\quad p_\theta = -n_\theta\sqrt{\Sigma},\quad L = -n_\phi\varpi,\quad E = \alpha + \omega L,$$

$$q = \frac{p_\theta^2 + \cos^2\theta\,(L^2/\sin^2\theta - a^2E^2)}{E^2}.$$

camera_beta moves the camera along $\mathbf e_\phi$ with speed $\beta$ relative to the ZAMO, which
applies special-relativistic aberration and a Doppler factor to every ray. The rays are traced
backwards (from the camera into the past).

passages.heading: The accretion disk
passages.text:
The disk is geometrically thin and optically thick, in the equatorial plane between $r_{\rm in}$ and
$r_{\rm out}$. By default $r_{\rm in}$ is the innermost stable circular orbit (Bardeen, Press & Teukolsky 1972):

$$Z_1 = 1 + (1-a^2)^{1/3}\left[(1+a)^{1/3} + (1-a)^{1/3}\right],\quad Z_2 = \sqrt{3a^2 + Z_1^2},$$
$$r_{\rm isco} = 3 + Z_2 \mp \sqrt{(3 - Z_1)(3 + Z_1 + 2Z_2)}\quad(6M \text{ for } a=0,\ 1.237M \text{ for } a = 0.998).$$

Temperature: Novikov–Thorne, with the flux of Page & Thorne (1974). The closed form in $x = \sqrt{r/M}$
(with $x_0 = \sqrt{r_{\rm isco}}$ and $x_{1,2,3}$ the roots of $x^3 - 3x + 2a = 0$) is

$$F = \frac{3\dot M}{8\pi M^2}\,\frac{1}{x^4(x^3 - 3x + 2a)}\left[x - x_0 - \tfrac32 a\ln\frac{x}{x_0}
- \sum_{i}\frac{3(x_i - a)^2}{x_i(x_i - x_j)(x_i - x_k)}\ln\frac{x - x_i}{x_0 - x_i}\right],$$

passages.heading: The accretion disk
passages.text:
and $T(r) = T_{\max}\,(F/F_{\max})^{1/4}$, where $T_{\max}$ is the parameter disk.temperature_scale. The flux is zero at
the ISCO (no torque on the inner edge), peaks just outside it and falls as $r^{-3/4}$ in temperature
far out. The code checks the closed form against a direct quadrature of the Page–Thorne integral,
$F = -\frac{\Omega_{,r}}{4\pi\sqrt{-g}(E-\Omega L)^2}\int_{r_{\rm isco}}^r (E - \Omega L)L_{,r}\,dr$
(they agree to $\le 7\times10^{-5}$ of the peak for $a \le 0.9$). disk.profile: "power_law" gives the
simpler $T \propto r^{-3/4}$ with a sharp inner edge instead.

Every crossing of the equatorial plane is located by Newton iteration on the cubic Hermite
interpolant of the accepted step. A crossing with $r_{\rm in} \le r \le r_{\rm out}$ is a disk hit. Any other
crossing (inside the ISCO or beyond the outer edge) lets the ray continue. This is what produces the
higher-order images: the far side of the disk bent over the top of the shadow, its underside bent
below it, and the thin photon ring that hugs the shadow (each extra half-orbit gives a fainter,
thinner copy). disk.opacity < 1 makes the disk semi-transparent: up to three hits are composited
front to back.

passages.heading: Frequency shift, colour and brightness
passages.text:
The gas follows prograde circular geodesics with $\Omega = 1/(r^{3/2} + a)$ and
$u^t = (r^{3/2} + a)/\left(r^{3/4}\sqrt{r^{3/2} - 3r^{1/2} + 2a}\right)$. A photon with $L = bE$ reaching a camera that
measures energy $E_{\rm cam}$ (for $E = 1$) has

$$g = \frac{\nu_{\rm obs}}{\nu_{\rm emit}} = \frac{E_{\rm cam}}{u^t\,(1 - \Omega b)}.$$

$g$ is split into a gravitational part, the lapse ratio $g_{\rm grav} = \alpha(r_{\rm emit})/\alpha(r_{\rm cam})$, and
the Doppler part $g/g_{\rm grav}$, which covers the orbital motion, frame dragging and any camera motion.

passages.heading: Frequency shift, colour and brightness
passages.text:
Since $I_\nu/\nu^3$ is invariant along a ray, a blackbody of temperature $T$ is seen as a blackbody of
temperature $gT$. The specific intensity scales as $I_\nu \propto g^3$, and the bolometric intensity as $g^4$.
The renderer therefore takes both colour and visible luminance from a blackbody at $gT$. The colour
is its CIE 1931 XYZ, integrated against Planck's law using the multi-lobe Gaussian fit of the
colour-matching functions by Wyman, Sloan & Shirley (2013), then converted to linear sRGB (D65).
This is computed once into a 512-entry table over $\log T$. The fit reproduces the Planckian locus to
better than $10^{-3}$ in $(x, y)$ (tested at 3000, 5000, 6500 and 10 000 K).

The toggles separate the effects:

| toggle | applies | to |

| disk.redshift | $g_{\rm grav}$ | colour and brightness |
| disk.doppler | $g/g_{\rm grav}$ | colour only |
| disk.beaming | $g/g_{\rm grav}$ | brightness only |
| interstellar: true | turns doppler and beaming off | |

passages.heading: Frequency shift, colour and brightness
passages.text:
Interstellar mode. James et al. (2015) write that the film's makers chose to omit the Doppler
shifts of the disk, so that the images would be understandable for a mass audience. Otherwise one
side of the disk is blue-white and much brighter than the other, as in the second image above. They
also lowered the spin to $a \approx 0.6$ for the disk shots. interstellar: true reproduces that choice;
the default keeps the physics complete.

passages.heading: Sky and image
passages.text:
Escaped rays sample a procedural celestial sphere in their asymptotic direction. Stars are **point
sources**. For every pixel, the Jacobian $J$ of the lens map (pixel → sky) comes from neighbouring
rays, and a star adds $\text{flux}\cdot e^{-q/2}\cdot\mu$, where $q$ is its distance from the pixel in
pixel units and $\mu = \text{pixel}^2/|\det J|$ is the magnification. Star images therefore stay about one
pixel wide however strongly the sky is sheared, and their brightness follows the magnification. This
is the job James et al. do with ray bundles. Near the shadow one pixel covers many star cells; there
the layer's mean surface brightness is used, since lensing conserves surface brightness. A star close
to the point directly behind the hole is drawn as an Einstein ring. Captured rays are black. The HDR
image then goes through a mild lens bloom, auto-exposure (99.5th percentile) for stills (held fixed
across an animation), the ACES filmic curve and sRGB encoding.

passages.heading: Sky and image
passages.text:
Animations. For animation: "orbit" the camera circles the hole in azimuth. The spacetime and the
disk are axisymmetric, so one trace serves every frame: only the sky rotation and the disk pattern
change. The disk pattern rotates differentially at the Keplerian $\Omega(r)$ and is sampled at the
emission time $t_{\rm cam} - \Delta t_{\rm ray}$, using the coordinate-time delay integrated along every ray, so
light-travel-time effects are in. zoom and inclination re-trace every frame.

passages.heading: What is approximated
passages.text:
* The disk is infinitely thin, stationary (apart from the cosmetic pattern) and emits isotropically
  as a blackbody. There is no limb darkening, no emission from the plunging region inside the ISCO,
  no returning radiation and no polarisation.
* The colour-matching functions are an analytic fit, not the tabulated CIE data (error < $10^{-3}$ in
  chromaticity).
* The stars and the faint band of light are procedural. Bloom is cosmetic.
* The browser version is limited to $a = 0$; see section 5.

passages.heading: From JEV (the agent)
passages.text:
Ask in plain language, for example "render the Interstellar black hole as a 10-second video" or
"show me a double pendulum and how fast the two runs diverge". The model calls these tools:

| tool | risk | what |

| render_black_hole | sandbox; asks first if a timing probe estimates > 10 min or frames × pixels × samples > 1920×1080×240 | PNG still or MP4/GIF + parameters JSON in <workspace>/science/ |
| simulate_physics | sandbox; asks if the estimate is > 10 min | MP4 + summary chart + metrics JSON |
| explain_black_hole_physics | read | the notes in jev/science/notes.py (topics: overview, geodesics, camera, disk, redshift, interstellar, shadow, limits, references) |

POST /api/jev/science/blackhole with the render parameters, and
POST /api/jev/science/simulate with {kind, params} (see api.md). Progress and the files
arrive on /api/jev/jobs/<id>/events.

passages.heading: Render parameters
passages.text:
Invalid values raise ValueError with a readable message. A cancelled render (cancelled() returns
true) returns [] and leaves no partial video behind. estimate_seconds(params) runs a 24×14 timing
probe. The JSON next to every output records the parameters, the trace statistics (mean steps per ray,
unresolved rays), the exposure, timings, the device and reference radii (horizon, ISCO, photon orbits).

passages.heading: 4. Performance (measured on this machine: 2 CPU cores, no GPU)
passages.text:
The runtime estimate behind the approval rule (estimate_seconds) uses a 32×18 probe trace for the
mean number of steps and a micro-benchmark of the geodesic right-hand side for this machine's cost per
step. Here it came out 0–35 % above the actual times; it errs long on purpose, since it decides when
to ask.

On a CUDA GPU the same code runs with device: "cuda". The tracer is a few hundred batched tensor
operations per step, so expect it to be one to two orders of magnitude faster at 1080p (not measured
here: no GPU on this machine). Shading (stars, colour) stays on the CPU in numpy.

passages.heading: 5. The browser version (`site/js/science/`)
passages.text:
* Supported: the Schwarzschild ($a = 0$) metric, exactly. Rays obey $u'' + u = 3Mu^2$, written as
  $\ddot{\mathbf x} = -3Mh^2\mathbf x/r^5$ and integrated by RK4 with steps proportional to $r$. The camera is a
  static observer with the correct aberration, so the shadow has the exact finite-distance size
  (checked in Chromium to 2 px). The disk has the Page–Thorne $a = 0$ temperature, Doppler / beaming /
  redshift toggles and Interstellar mode, and the same blackbody colour table as Python
  (color.js, tested for parity). Stars are point sources with Jacobian-based magnification (from
  dFdx / dFdy); the checker grid and no background are also available. Quality is low / medium /
  high (render scale 0.5 / 0.75 / 1 and 220 / 360 / 700 steps). You can orbit with drag, zoom with the
  wheel or a pinch, or use the keyboard (arrows, + / −, space to auto-rotate). It respects
  prefers-reduced-motion (no rotation or disk animation; it renders only on change).
* Desktop only: spin (frame dragging, the asymmetric Kerr shadow), light-travel-time delays,
  supersampling and video output. capabilities.spin === false tells the UI to say so.
* Without WebGL2 mountBlackHole throws an Error whose message mentions WebGL2, so the caller
  can show its own fallback. Pass fallback: 'message' to draw a message on the canvas instead.

passages.heading: JEV and Science in the app (front end)
passages.text:
The JEV tab and the Science tab are part of the one static front end in site/, shared by the
website and the desktop app. This page describes what they show, how they talk to the local
backend (api.md), and the accessibility and security rules they follow. For what the
agent may do on its own, see SAFETY.md.

| Tab | Web (GitHub Pages) | Desktop app |

| JEV | A panel that says JEV needs the desktop app, links to the release downloads, lists what JEV can do and the three risk levels, and sends you to Science | Chat with streaming answers, tool cards, approvals and the audit log, files, status strip, Models, Settings and Doctor |
| Science | Live black hole and simulations (WebGL) | The same, plus "Render on this computer": an MP4 rendered by the backend, with progress |

The tab bar puts JEV and Science first, then a divider, then the JEPA workflow (Data, Train,
Inspect, Evaluate, World model, Explain, Export). With no #tab in the address and no remembered
tab, the desktop app opens on JEV and the website on Data (the JEPA demo that runs in a browser).
The JEPA progress stepper is hidden on JEV and Science.

passages.heading: Talking to the backend
passages.text:
Every call goes through DesktopBackend (site/js/backend.js), which exists only when the shell
injected window.__JEPA_DESKTOP__ = {port, token}. The website never constructs it, so a visitor's
browser never tries to reach a local port (and the site's CSP, connect-src 'self', would block
it anyway).

Routes the UI uses (all in api.md):

| Feature | Routes |

passages.heading: Talking to the backend
passages.text:
| Status strip, Doctor | GET /status every 15 s while the page is visible; GET /models |
| Chat | POST /chat, then GET /turns/<id>/events?since=n every 200 ms (900 ms while an approval is pending) until done, error or cancelled; POST /turns/<id>/cancel for Stop |
| Conversations | GET /conversations, GET /conversations/<id>, POST /conversations (an empty one, before the first upload), DELETE /conversations/<id> (answered with an approval), GET /conversations/<id>/export |
| Attachments | POST /conversations/<id>/files with {name, mime, data_base64}; files over 1.5 MB are refused in the page, because the base64 body must stay under the 2 MB cap. The returned path goes into attachments of the next POST /chat |
| Approvals | GET /approvals?status=pending every 3 s while visible, GET /approvals?limit=5000 for the history (audit log), POST /approvals/<id> with {decision, remember, args_sha256} (the hash of the exact arguments the card showed; required to approve) |
| Models | GET /models (installed + imported SHA-256s), POST /settings {default_model}, POST /models/pull, POST /models/import {gguf_path, name} (the path comes from the shell's pick_gguf_file), DELETE /models/<name>; the last three answer with an approval, and after "Approve" the job_id in the decision's response is followed with GET /jobs/<id>/events |
| Settings | GET /settings (settings, rules, paths), POST /settings with only the changed keys, GET /export (a zip, saved with a normal download), POST /data/delete {keep_audit_log} (answered with an approval); sandbox facts come from GET /status |
| Files | GET /artifacts/<id> with the token header, shown through a blob: URL |
| Science renders | POST /science/blackhole, POST /science/simulate, then GET /jobs/<id>/events; a long render answers with an approval first |

passages.heading: Talking to the backend
passages.text:
The approval decision's response carries job_id when approving starts a job (model downloads,
imports, deletes, long renders), so the page can follow its progress. If the approval table is
set to run for that row, the request itself answers {status: "auto_run", job_id} and the page
follows the job directly.

passages.heading: Streaming without flooding screen readers
passages.text:
The conversation is a role="log" region with aria-live="polite" and
aria-relevant="additions". While a turn runs:

* the log has aria-busy="true", and the text that streams in token by token is
  aria-hidden="true";
* one short message per tool step ("Running render_black_hole.", "run_shell needs your approval.")
  goes to a separate, visually hidden role="status" line. Nothing is announced per token.

When the turn ends, the streamed text is replaced by the formatted answer (a new node), the log's
aria-busy turns false, and one sentence is appended for screen readers: "JEV answered after
2 tool calls: …" (the first 280 characters). The log keeps itself scrolled to the newest content
while you are at the bottom, and stays put when you scroll up to read.

passages.heading: Tool cards
The approval dialog
passages.text:
When a request arrives (from a turn's approval_request event or the pending list) and you are on
the JEV or Science tab, a modal <dialog> opens; on another tab, a notice with a Review button
appears and the JEV tab shows the count. The dialog shows:

passages.heading: The approval dialog
passages.text:
* a question naming the action ("Allow JEV to run a command on your computer?", "… to download a
  model?", "… to delete something?", "… to use the internet?", …) and one sentence on what will
  happen;
* the exact command, path, address or model in a monospace block, so you approve what will
  actually run; all arguments, never cut, are one click away ("All arguments", scrollable), with
  the SHA-256 of those exact arguments, computed in the page over the canonical JSON the backend
  sent (after checking it is exactly what the card shows). Invisible and text-direction characters
  (U+202E, zero-width spaces, control characters) are shown as visible \uXXXX escapes, with a
  warning. Approving sends the page's own hash (`POST /approvals/<id> {decision, remember,
  args_sha256}`) and the backend refuses an approval whose hash does not match the pending call;
* why it asks (the backend's reason) and the tool with its risk badge;
* Deny, Approve for this session, Approve once. "For this session" covers only these
  exact arguments of this tool in this conversation; shell commands, installs, network use,
  deletes, models and paths outside the workspace are asked every time. Focus starts on Deny. Esc is Deny
  (the dialog's cancel event). Tab moves between the buttons; focus returns to where it was when
  the dialog closes. With several requests waiting, it says "1 of 3 requests" and shows the next
  after each answer.

passages.heading: The approval dialog
passages.text:
If the answer cannot be saved, the dialog stays open and says so. If the backend reports that the
request was already decided, or that the approved action failed to start, a notice says that
instead of "Approved".

"N waiting" appears as a count on the JEV tab (its accessible name becomes "JEV, 2 approvals
waiting") and on the Approvals button, until every request is answered. The Approvals panel
lists pending requests (each with Review) and the audit history: time, tool, the exact command or
path, and the decision with an icon and a word (Approved, Denied, Ran automatically, Expired, …).

passages.heading: Models panel
passages.text: Models (in the status strip, or Manage models next to the model menu) opens a sheet with:

passages.heading: Models panel
passages.text:
* Installed: one row per Ollama model with its size, parameter count, quantization, family
  and the first 12 characters of Ollama's digest (the full digest is the tooltip); a GGUF you
  imported also shows the SHA-256 JEV recorded for the file. Make default saves
  default_model and selects it in the composer; Delete… asks (the dialog names the model).
* Download a model: a name field and Request download (asks, then a progress bar).
  Below it, examples that fit this computer: the tier for the largest GPU memory in
  status.gpu.devices (CPU only or under 6 GB, 6 to 11, 12 to 23, 24 GB and more; an Apple GPU
  counts as the 6 to 11 tier) and the next smaller tier, each with its approximate download
  size, whether it is already installed, and a note on models without native tool calling.
  Clicking one only fills the name; nothing downloads without the approval.
* Import a GGUF file: Choose a .gguf file… calls the shell's pick_gguf_file. The page
  never supplies a path: the native dialog returns one, and the shell has already granted the
  backend that single file after checking its name and GGUF header. The panel proposes a
  name from the file name (lowercase, other characters as -), validates it like the backend
  (MODEL_NAME), and Request import asks. When the job finishes the recorded SHA-256 is
  shown. Without the shell (no window.TAURI), the button is disabled and the reason gives
  the jev models import command.
* Where the model files are: Ollama's default folder per OS and how to move it with
  OLLAMA_MODELS.

passages.heading: Settings panel
passages.text:
Settings opens a form for the keys the API may change, each validated in the page with
the backend's bounds before Save settings is enabled (errors are next to the field, linked
with aria-describedby, and the field gets aria-invalid); only changed keys are sent:

* default model (the installed models, plus the current value if it is not installed);
* Ollama address: must be loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1, localhost). Another address needs
  Allow an Ollama on another machine, which shows a warning that prompts and files would
  leave the computer, and is still refused while allow_remote_ollama is off in the file (the
  message names the settings file): the page cannot turn that switch on;
* the five sandbox limits (cpu_seconds, wall_seconds, memory_mb, max_output_mb,
  max_file_mb), whole numbers within jev/settings.py's bounds;
* network_allowed, explained: it lifts the sandbox's network block and skips that one
  question, while downloads, installs, shell commands, sending data and deleting still ask.

passages.heading: Settings panel
passages.text:
Below the form, read only: what the sandbox enforces here (network and file isolation, method,
resource limits, how runaway code is stopped, from status.sandbox); Your data, the paths of
the data folder, database, settings file, workspaces and exports with Copy buttons (the shell
has no command to open folders, on purpose), Export all data (.zip) and Delete all data…
(asks; "Keep the audit log" is a checkbox); the approval table (rule, what it covers, the
current action with an icon and a word, the default when you changed it, Locked rows); and the
settings only the file can change.

passages.heading: Audit log
passages.text:
The Approvals panel's History (audit log) loads up to 5 000 decisions and filters them in
the page by decision (Approved by you, Denied by you, Ran automatically, Refused by policy,
Waiting, Expired / cancelled / failed), tool and a date range (local days, inclusive), with a
count ("2 of 5 decisions"). Export CSV saves the filtered rows with every field (ids, ISO
times, status, decided_by, rules, reason, arguments as JSON); a cell that would start with =,
+, - or @ gets a leading ' so a spreadsheet never runs it as a formula. Below 620 px
each row stacks: time and decision, tool, then what it did.

passages.heading: Files (artifacts)
passages.text:
Images (with a lightbox: Esc closes it and focus returns), videos (<video controls>), audio
(<audio controls>), code and text (highlighted, line numbers drawn by CSS so copying copies no
numbers), other files as a download. Downloads are ` links on the same blob:` URL.
File names and titles are always inserted as text. Object URLs are revoked when you switch
conversation.

Content Security Policy for this: the website and the desktop shell both allow
img-src 'self' data: blob: and media-src 'self' blob:; connect-src is unchanged
('self' on the web; 'self' plus the one backend port on the desktop, see
../desktop.md).

passages.heading: Status strip and Doctor
passages.text:
The strip shows, each with an icon and words: Ollama running (and its version) or not reachable;
the chosen model or "No model yet"; whether sandboxed code is offline (sandbox.network_isolation
is "enforced") or could reach the network; the GPU from gpu.devices (or "CPU only").

Doctor turns the same facts into checks with fixes: install and start Ollama, download a model,
what missing network isolation means. Commands are shown for macOS, Windows or Linux (guessed from
the browser, switchable, remembered) with Copy buttons; links are given as text because the
desktop window does not open external pages. When /api/jev/status does not answer, Doctor says
whether the backend lacks the JEV routes (HTTP 404) or did not respond, and uses the shell's own
Ollama probe (backend_status().ollama) as a second opinion.

Send stays disabled, with the reason under the box, until the backend answers, Ollama is reachable
and a model is chosen.

passages.heading: Science tab
passages.text:
The tab loads site/js/science/blackhole.js and sims.js with a dynamic import() only when it is
shown, and destroys the view when you leave the tab or hide the page (a fresh <canvas> each
time, since a destroyed WebGL context cannot be reused). If a module is missing or WebGL cannot
start, the stage shows a plain explanation and a Try again button instead.

The UI calls:

const bh = mountBlackHole(canvas, { reducedMotion, spin, distance, inclination, disk, doppler, beaming, quality });
bh.setParams({ spin, distance, inclination, disk, doppler, beaming, quality });  // on every change
bh.snapshot();   // Blob | data URL | canvas; the PNG is saved with a normal download
bh.destroy();

const sim = mountSim(canvas, kind, { reducedMotion, ...params });   // kind: nbody | double_pendulum | wave
sim.setParams(params); sim.reset(); sim.destroy();

passages.heading: Science tab
passages.text:
distance is in units of M, inclination in degrees from the spin axis, quality is low,
medium or high. Simulation parameters: nbody {bodies, speed}, double_pendulum
{theta1, theta2, massRatio, speed} (degrees), wave {speed, damping, freq}. If the module
says it cannot draw spin (capabilities.spin === false on the handle or the module), a note
under the slider says so and that rendering on the computer uses it.

"Render high-quality video on this computer" (desktop) posts the same settings in the backend's
units (spin, inclination_deg, distance_M, disk: {enabled, doppler, beaming}, width,
height, seconds, frames, quality: "final"; simulations as {kind, params} with
jev/science/sims.py's names), follows the job, and lists the MP4 in the tab's own Files list.

passages.heading: The web demo tier
passages.text:
The website (site/, published at <https://normansrule.github.io/jev-jepa-studio/>) is the same
front end as the JEV Studio desktop app. In a browser it trains a real LeJEPA model inside the tab.
It is a demo: small enough to finish in a few minutes on a laptop CPU, faithful enough that the
loss, the collapse detector and the evaluation behave like the desktop app. For real models, use
the desktop app.

passages.heading: JEV and Science on the website
passages.text:
* JEV, the local AI agent, needs a language model served by Ollama on your computer and a
  backend that can run code, so it only works in the desktop app. On the website the JEV tab says
  so, links to the installers, and lists what JEV can do and its three risk levels. The page never
  tries to contact a local port: the backend client exists only in the desktop app, and the site's
  Content Security Policy (connect-src 'self') would block it anyway.
* Science works here: the black hole and the simulations are drawn live on your graphics card
  with WebGL. Without WebGL the tab explains why and shows nothing else. Rendering long,
  high-resolution videos needs the desktop app. Details: jev/ui.md.

passages.heading: What trains in the browser
passages.text:
The encoder is mlp-tiny: each view is resampled to 16×16 RGB, standardized per channel, and
flattened to 768 numbers.

* backbone: Linear(768 → 256), GELU, Linear(256 → 64). The 64-d output is the embedding used
  by Inspect, Evaluate and Export.
* projector: Linear(64 → 64), GELU, Linear(64 → 16). The LeJEPA loss is applied to this 16-d output.

GELU is the exact erf form, like PyTorch's default. Differences from the desktop app: the web
projector has two layers and no BatchNorm (the desktop projector has three layers with
BatchNorm), and SIGReg uses 64 random directions per step by default instead of 256.

passages.heading: The loss, exactly
passages.text:
For a batch of N images with V views each (Vg of them global), and projections z:

* centres: the mean projection of the global views of each image.
* prediction term L_pred: the mean over views, images and dimensions of (centre − z)².
* SIGReg: for each view, draw M random unit directions, project the batch onto each, and
  compute the Epps–Pulley statistic of the N projected values against N(0, 1); average over
  directions and views.
* total: L = (1 − λ) L_pred + λ SIGReg, with λ = 0.05 by default.

The Epps–Pulley statistic compares the empirical characteristic function of the projected
values with exp(−t²/2) at 17 frequencies t in [0, 3], weighted by exp(−t²/2), trapezoid rule,
times N. Under a perfect Gaussian its expected value is about 1.05, so SIGReg values near 1
mean "Gaussian". A collapsed embedding gives values in the tens or hundreds.

The JavaScript loss matches jepa_studio.losses.lejepa_loss to 1e-4 on the same inputs and
directions (tests/test_web_engine.py), and its hand-written gradient is checked against finite
differences (tests/js/engine_gradcheck.mjs).

passages.heading: Why SIGReg prevents collapse
passages.text:
The prediction term alone is minimized by mapping every input to the same vector: all views
then agree perfectly. SIGReg makes that impossible, because a batch of identical vectors
projects to a single spike, which is as far from N(0, 1) as a distribution can be. Requiring
every random 1-D projection to look like N(0, 1) forces the embeddings to spread out with equal
variance in every direction (an isotropic Gaussian), by the Cramér–Wold theorem.

passages.heading: Reading the collapse detector
passages.text:
The Inspect tab computes the covariance of the projector outputs of up to 1024 images.

* effective rank: exp of the entropy of the normalized eigenvalues, from 1 (one direction) to 16.
* isotropy ratio: smallest eigenvalue divided by the largest.
* complete collapse: the mean standard deviation is below 0.001.
* dimensional collapse: effective rank below max(1.5, 10% of the dimension), or one direction
  holds more than 90% of the variance.
* anisotropic: isotropy ratio below 0.01.
* healthy: none of the above.

A short demo run usually reports "anisotropic" or "dimensional collapse" in its first few
dozen steps and moves toward healthy as SIGReg does its work. Raising λ speeds this up at the
cost of the prediction term.

passages.heading: Batch size and the timing probe
passages.text:
With batch size "auto", the app times one training step at batch 32, 64, 128, 256 and keeps
the largest batch whose step stays under 150 ms. 32 is the floor: with fewer samples the
Epps–Pulley statistic of each direction is too noisy to be a useful signal.

passages.heading: WebGPU
passages.text:
When the browser exposes WebGPU, the two largest products (the first layer's forward pass and
its weight gradient) run as compute shaders. The app checks the shaders against the JavaScript
result and times both paths at start-up; it only uses WebGPU when it is correct and faster.
The header badge says which backend is active: "WebGPU" or "CPU (JavaScript)". Software
adapters (for example SwiftShader in headless browsers) are usually slower than JavaScript and
are rejected.

passages.heading: Linear probe and k-NN
passages.text:
Evaluate freezes the encoder and uses its 64-d embeddings of un-augmented images. 20% of the
images are held out; a labeled subset (10% of the rest by default) trains the classifiers.

* linear probe: softmax regression on standardized features, full-batch AdamW for 100 epochs.
* k-NN: cosine similarity, k = 20, majority vote; ties go to the class of the single most
  similar neighbour.
* random-init baseline: the same MLP with untrained weights.
* supervised baseline: the same MLP trained end-to-end with cross-entropy on the labeled subset.

passages.heading: Your files
passages.text:
Images and CSV files are read with the File API and decoded in the page. Nothing is uploaded:
the page's Content Security Policy only allows requests to its own origin. Limits: 2000 images,
20 MB and 40 megapixels per image, 20 MB per CSV.

Three ways in, all through the same loader and the same limits:

* the Choose images…, Choose a folder… and Choose CSV… buttons (the keyboard route);
* drag and drop onto the drop zone at the top of the Data tab: image files, a whole folder
  (walked with webkitGetAsEntry, up to 8 levels deep), or a CSV file. Dropping class folders
  side by side (cats/, dogs/) labels the images like a folder of class folders; a CSV switches
  to Time series. A drop replaces the current image set;
* paste (Ctrl+V / ⌘V) with the drop zone focused, or anywhere on the Data tab outside a text
  field. Pasted images are added to the current set, so you can paste screenshots one at a time;
  the status line counts them until there are the 16 that training needs.

The drop zone is a focusable button: Enter or Space opens the matching file picker.

passages.heading: Entering settings
passages.text:
* Precise values. Every slider has a number box with the same minimum, maximum and step,
  synced both ways. The number is the value used: typing 35 steps into a slider that moves in
  tens trains 35 steps (the slider shows the nearest position). Arrow keys step the box; Enter
  or leaving the box applies it.
* Inline validation against the shared schema. Each control knows its config key
  (train.max_steps, objective.lambda, seed…) and is checked with the same validate() and
  config.schema.json the desktop app uses, then against the range this tier offers (the web
  demo runs 20–2000 steps). A bad value gets a message under the field (aria-invalid,
  aria-describedby), is never applied or clamped, and Start stays disabled with the reason
  shown next to it ("Fix Steps and Seed (Data tab) to start.").
* Reset to defaults next to each section heading restores the values of
  webDefaultConfig() in site/js/config.js.
* Presets on the Train tab set steps, batch size and SIGReg directions and put λ and the
  learning rate back to their defaults. Changing any of those afterwards shows "Custom".

  | Preset | Web demo | Desktop app |

* Help. The ⓘ button next to a label opens a short explanation with a link to the matching

passages.heading: The run config editor
passages.text:
The Export tab shows the current run config as formatted JSON. Edit it, then:

* Validate parses it, merges it onto the defaults and checks it against the schema, exactly
  like opening a file (and like jepa_studio.config.load_config). Problems are listed under the
  editor with their paths ($.objective.lambda: 2 > maximum 1); clicking one selects that key.
  A JSON syntax error says which line and column.
* Apply (or Ctrl+Enter) sends a valid config to the Data and Train tabs.
* Revert discards the edits; Download saves the applied config (disabled while there
  are unapplied edits, and it says so); Open config… loads a file into the editor and
  applies it when valid. If you have unapplied edits, it asks before replacing them.

The file format is the desktop app's, so a config saved here opens there unchanged.

passages.heading: Guidance and preferences
passages.text:
* A progress strip under the tabs (Data → Train → Inspect → Evaluate → Export) marks each step
  done from what has actually happened: data chosen, a run finished, embeddings inspected, an
  evaluation run, something exported. A new run starts the later steps over.
* When a run ends, the Train tab offers the next step ("Inspect the embeddings"). Completions and
  errors also appear as short notices in the corner (announced to screen readers: errors as
  alerts, the rest politely); the panels keep their own text too.
* Inspect, Evaluate and Export say what to do first when there is no model yet, and disabled
  buttons say why they are disabled.
* The theme, the last tab and the last preset are remembered per browser in localStorage.
  When storage is unavailable (private windows, blocked site data) the app works the same and
  simply forgets them.

passages.heading: World model and planning bot
passages.text:
A JEPA world model learns, from pixels and actions only, to predict the embedding of the next
frame. A planner then searches for actions whose imagined embeddings reach the embedding of a
goal image. Code: jepa_studio/world/ (Python) and site/js/world/ (the browser port).
Recipe: LeWorldModel (Maes et al., arXiv:2603.19312), re-implemented at toy scale.

jepa-studio world --env two-room            # train + evaluate + export, into runs/world-two-room/
jepa-studio world --env push-block --out runs/world-push-block

passages.heading: 1. Environments (`world/envs.py`)
passages.text:
Two tiny, deterministic 2-D worlds rendered as 32 × 32 RGB images. Both are pure
(step(state, action) never mutates anything), and reset(seed) uses the mulberry32 generator,
so Python and the browser replay the same trajectories (tests/test_world_parity.py).

| | two-room | push-block |

passages.heading: 1. Environments (`world/envs.py`)
passages.text:
| picture | a red agent dot; a vertical wall at x = 0.5 with a door around y = 0.5 | a red agent dot and a blue square block in an open arena |
| state | agent (x, y) | agent (x, y), block (x, y) |
| action | velocity in $[-1, 1]^2$, × 0.08 arena units per step | same |
| dynamics | the wall blocks the agent except through the door (agent radius 0.04, door half-height 0.12) | a kinematic push: overlapping the block moves it along the axis of least penetration; a block stuck at the border pushes the agent back |
| goal | a point in either room, 0.2–0.6 from the start | the block moved 0.1–0.2 along one axis, agent resting behind it |
| success | agent within 0.08 of the goal | block within 0.06 of its goal position (agent anywhere) |
| exploration data | smoothed random walk; in about half the episodes it first heads through the door | in about 75% of episodes, walk behind the block and push for a few steps, repeatedly; otherwise a random walk |

passages.heading: 2. Model (`world/model.py`)
passages.text:
$$
z_t = f(o_t), \qquad \hat z_{t+1} = g(z_t, a_t) = z_t + \operatorname{MLP}([z_t, a_t])
$$

* Encoder $f$: fixed input standardisation (the mean training image and one scalar pixel
  standard deviation, stored as buffers), three stride-2 4 × 4 convolutions (32 → 16 → 8 → 4 px,
  16/32/32 channels, ReLU), then Linear → ReLU → Linear to $z \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$. No BatchNorm, so a
  single frame can be encoded on its own (and in the browser). Kaiming initialisation. Without the
  input standardisation, frames that are ~95% background map to nearly the same latent at
  initialisation and training stays collapsed (see the ConvEncoder docstring).
* Predictor $g$: residual MLP on the concatenation of latent and action, 2 hidden layers of 64
  ReLU units. The last layer starts at zero, so an untrained predictor is the "nothing changes"
  (copy) baseline.
* The shipped models: $d = 16$, 99 568 parameters each.

passages.heading: 3. Training (the two-term loss)
passages.text:
For a window of $W$ consecutive frames and the $W-1$ actions between them (world_loss):

$$
\mathcal{L} = (1-\lambda)\,\underbrace{\operatorname{mean}_{b,k,j}\bigl(\hat z_k - z_k\bigr)^2}_{\text{open-loop prediction}}
+ \lambda\,\underbrace{\operatorname{SIGReg}\bigl(\{z\}{B \cdot W}\bigr)}{\text{latents} \to \mathcal{N}(0, I)}
$$

where $\hat z_k = g^k(z_0, a_0..a_{k-1})$ is rolled out from the first frame only (open loop,
$k = 1..W-1$), exactly how the planner uses the model. There is no decoder, no reconstruction
loss, no EMA target network and no stop-gradient: gradients flow into the targets $z_k$ too
(tests/test_world.py::test_gradients_flow_through_targets). The prediction term alone is
minimised by a constant encoder; SIGReg (the same losses.SIGReg as pretraining) forbids it.

Settings for the shipped models (HPARAMS_BY_ENV; not part of the shared config schema):

| | two-room | push-block |

| episodes × length | 400 × 24 | 800 × 24 |
| window $W$ (open-loop steps) | 6 (5) | 8 (7) |
| batch (windows) | 48 | 32 |
| $\lambda$, SIGReg slices | 0.2, 64 | 0.2, 64 |
| steps, learning rate | 3000, 2e-3 (100 warm-up, cosine to 1%) | same |

The world block of the run config holds only the environment, data and planner keys
(env, episodes, episode_len, horizon, cem_samples, cem_elites, cem_iters); the
default episodes is 400. Without --config, jepa-studio world --env <env> uses the same
episode budget as the shipped models (EPISODES_BY_ENV: two-room 400, push-block 800). To
rebuild the shipped artifacts exactly, run

jepa-studio world --env push-block --site
# or both at once:
python -c "from jepa_studio.world import build_site_models; build_site_models()"

which retrains both, rewrites site/models/world-*.json, site/models/world-metrics.json,
runs/world-*/ and the two GIFs in assets/. 10% of the episodes are held out for the
prediction and collapse metrics.

passages.heading: 4. Planner (`world/planner.py`)
passages.text:
The Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) with receding horizon: plan $H$ = 5 steps with 300 samples, 30
elites and 10 rounds, execute only the first action in the real environment, re-encode the
new real frame, replan (warm-started from the previous plan shifted by one step). An episode
ends at success or after 40 steps. The cost is the summed squared distance of the imagined
latents to the goal latent. Every formula, with a worked example, is in
equations.md §5.

Imagination is shown by retrieval, not generation. A JEPA has no decoder, so imagined
latents cannot be turned into pixels. The GIFs and the World tab show, for each imagined
latent, the real training frame whose embedding is nearest (a bank of 1024 encoded real
frames), and label it "retrieval, not generation".

What this does and doesn't show:

passages.heading: 5. Results (from `runs/world-*/metrics.json`)
passages.text:
* two-room works: the planner reaches the goal in 16 of 20 episodes, versus 3 of 20 for random
  actions, and ends much closer on average.
* push-block is weak. CEM solves 5 of 20 episodes (random: 0), but its mean final block
  distance (0.189) is worse than random (0.158) and worse than not moving at all (0.151): when it
  fails, it often pushes the block the wrong way. The latent encodes the block's position poorly
  (R² 0.19 / 0.38), which is the likely bottleneck. Treat it as an honest baseline to improve on.
* 20 episodes is a small sample; one seed, one training run per environment. These are toy
  environments at toy scale, meant to show the mechanism, not to compare with published numbers.
* The GIFs (assets/world-two-room.gif, assets/world-push-block.gif) show the **first
  CEM-solved evaluation episode** for each environment, chosen on purpose to illustrate a
  success. The success rates above are the representative numbers.

passages.heading: 6. In the browser
passages.text:
world/export.py writes each model as plain JSON (format: jepa-studio-world/v1: layer
weights rounded to 6 significant digits, the retrieval bank, the planner defaults and the
metrics). The web app's World model tab loads site/models/world-<env>.json and runs the
encoder, predictor and CEM in JavaScript: no ONNX, no WebGL. The weights are rounded before
evaluation, so the metrics above, world.safetensors and the JSON describe the same model, and
tests/test_world_parity.py checks the JavaScript encoder, predictor and environments against
PyTorch. The web tier can plan with the shipped models; training a new world model needs the
command line or the desktop app.
